Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
WMU 332 Aerial Ungulate Survey for Moose (2018) 
 
Background 
An aerial ungulate survey for moose was conducted in December 2018 in Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 332 
using transect survey methodology. This WMU is located in the Lower Foothills Natural Region of west central 
Alberta and is 2,870 km2. Prior to 2018, WMU 332 was surveyed in 1987, 1999, 2000, 2002, 2007 and 2011 using 
a random stratified block methodology. The population and density estimates were determined as a proportion of 
the total survey based on WMU area. 
  
During the 2018 aerial survey, sightings of white-tailed deer, mule deer and elk were recorded and population 
estimates were completed for these three species as well using transect survey methodology. Population 
estimates for white-tailed deer, mule deer and elk were calculated previously for WMU 332 during the 1999, 2000 
and 2002 aerial surveys. All of these above observations were recorded and enter ed into the Fisheries and 
Wildlife Management Information System (FWMIS) at the completion of the survey.  
 
In WMU 332, the antlered and antlerless moose archery only season runs from September 1 to October 31 and 
the general (rifle) season runs from November 1 to 30. Both the archery only and the general (rifle) require 
Special Licences obtained through the Special Licence application process.  
   
Hunter harvest data in WMU 332 for moose Special Licences indicate five-year (2014 to 2018) average success 
as follows: antlered moose 60% and antlerless moose 61%. Over the past five-years on average, 48 Antlered 
Moose Special Licences were issued annually and 28 Special Licences annually were issued for antlerless 
moose. 
  
The primary objectives of this survey were to assess the status of moose populations in WMU 332 by determining 
a population estimate based on density estimates, and a population demographic split for sex and age classes.  
The secondary objectives of this survey were to assess the status of white -tailed deer, mule deer and elk 
populations in WMU 332 by determining a population estimate based on density estimates, and a population 
demographic split for sex and age classes. 
 
Survey Method 
The transect survey was conducted flying east-west lines at 1.6 kilometre (1 mile) intervals, with 25% coverage 
(400 metre wide survey strip) in December 2018 on the following dates: 
 
 December 4 (5.5 flight hours) 
 December 5 (7.4 flight hours) 
 December 6 (7.8 flight hours) 
 December 7 (1.0 flight hours) 
 
The entire survey required 21.7 flight hours to complete. Throughout the duration of the survey, snow conditions 
were excellent and there were lights winds (<10 km/hr) each day. At each observation point, we counted moose 
and we determined sex and age and verified that each observation was within the transect width. For white-tailed 
deer, mule deer and elk we classified each observation for sex and age class, but did not record antler size.

Because transects varied in length (see Krebs 2014, Jolly 1969), we calculated the average density (R; #/km 2) of 
moose by summing the total animals counted per transect (∑x) by total area searched (length of transects 
multiplied by 400 metre survey strip [∑z]). For a population estimate (unequal sized units, sampling without 
replacement), we multiplied the average density (R) by the overall area of the WMU (Z). No correction factor was 
applied for moose population estimates. We calculated the width of the 90% confidenc e interval by multiplying the 
t-statistic for the left-tailed inverse of the Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; without 
replacement) of the abundance estimate where SE=sq root variance, and variance=N*(N -n)/(n*(n-
1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-2*R*∑xz) with N as the total number of possible transects given 100% coverage, and n as the 
number of transects sampled. 
 
Results 
For WMU 332 we surveyed 44 transects out of a possible 176 on December 4  to 7, 2018 for a total survey effort 
of 1,775 kilometres of transects and a survey area of 789.93 km 2 (24.73% of WMU). In total, we counted 289 
moose from 152 groups. Of the 289 moose that were classified: 
  
 77 (27%) were bulls 
 135 (46%) were cows 
 77 (27%) were calves  
 
The bull:cow and calf:cow ratios were 0.57 and 0.57, respectively. The final density estimate was 0.41/km 2 with a 
90% confidence interval of 0.34/km2 to 0.48 km2. This corresponds to a 90% confidence interval that is +/- 16% of 
the density estimate. The estimated moose abundance is 1,168 (983, 1354). We estimated the 2018 post-hunting 
season winter moose population split to be:  
 
 315 bulls 
 537 cows 
 315 calves

Survey effort parameters for white-tailed deer, mule deer and elk were identical to what was surveyed for moose 
and outlined above.  Population estimates were calculated for white-tailed deer, mule deer and elk using the 
same methodology as outlined for moose (see Krebs 2014, Jolly 1969) for transects of varying lengths.   
 
A total of 744 white-tailed deer were observed; 736 were classified. Of the white-tailed deer observed and 
classified, there were:  
 
 76 (10%) bucks 
 437 (59%) does 
 223 (30%) fawns   
 
There were 8 white-tailed deer unclassified. The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were .17 and .51 respectively.   
 
The final density estimate for white-tailed deer was 1.05 /km2 for a final post-hunting season winter estimate of 
3,008 white-tailed deer. We estimated the post-hunting season winter population split to be: 
 
 301 bucks 
 1,805 does 
 902 fawns

A total of 59 mule deer were observed in six groups. Of the mule deer classified observed there were:  
 
 12 (20%) bucks 
 32 (54%) does 
 15 (25%) fawns  
 
The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were .38 and .47 respectively. The final density estimate for mule deer was 
0.08 /km2 for a final post-hunting season winter estimate of 121 mule deer. We estimated the post-hunting season 
winter population split to be:  
 
 25 bucks 
 65 does 
 31 fawns

A total of 186 elk were observed in twelve groups. Due to the low number of groups (12) of elk which were 
observed it is problematic to provide a statistically reliable population estimate for elk.  Based on surveying 25% 
of the WMU, and observing 186 elk, a simplistic density estimate 0.26 elk/km2 which equates to a population 
estimate of 752 elk. Of the 186 elk observed there were 12 bulls, 87 cows and 35 calves classified and 52 elk 
were not classified.
